title: 24 Ways to Embed Retrieval Practice in Your Classroom
subtitle: Evidence-informed strategies, with or without technology · Rooted in the work of Bjork, Roediger & Karpicke, Agarwal, Dunlosky, Cepeda, Kornell, Rohrer, Ebbinghaus, Kapur and Metcalfe
scholars: Rooted in the work of Bjork, Roediger & Karpicke, Agarwal, Dunlosky, Cepeda, Kornell, Rohrer, Ebbinghaus, Kapur, Metcalfe, Nestojko, Fiorella & Mayer, Slamecka & Graf and Godden & Baddeley
quote: "The act of retrieving knowledge is itself a learning event, not merely a test of what has been learned." — Roediger & Karpicke, 2006
research: Rooted in the work of Bjork, Roediger & Karpicke, Agarwal, Dunlosky, Cepeda, Kornell, Rohrer, Ebbinghaus, Kapur, Metcalfe, Nestojko, Fiorella & Mayer, Slamecka & Graf and Godden & Baddeley

strategies.title: Retrieval Beats Re-reading
strategies.summary: Replace re-reading with retrieval. Instead of reviewing notes, ask students to write down everything they remember, then check. The testing is the learning, not the preparation for it.

strategies.title: Low-Stakes Starter Quizzes
strategies.summary: Five questions per lesson on prior content; nothing in the gradebook. Agarwal found routine quizzing reduces test anxiety rather than causing it. The quiz is not the assessment. It is the learning.

strategies.title: Brain Dump
strategies.summary: A blank page, two minutes, no notes: write everything you remember. The imperfect attempt is the point. What students cannot recall shows precisely where teaching needs to return.

strategies.title: Test Before You Teach
strategies.summary: Quiz students before teaching. Struggling to retrieve primes the brain; students who fail before instruction remember the answer more reliably once taught. Failure is productive.

strategies.title: Closed-Book Reconstruction
strategies.summary: Students reconstruct key ideas from memory, then open notes and correct in a different colour. Karpicke and Blunt found this outperforms re-reading. The corrections are the data.

strategies.title: Distribute Practice Over Time
strategies.summary: Spread retrieval across days and weeks rather than cramming it into one session. Build review points into your medium-term plan. The calendar is part of the pedagogy.

strategies.title: Yesterday, Last Week, Last Month
strategies.summary: Three questions per lesson: one from yesterday, one from last week, one from last month. These intervals are a starting point; complex topics may need revisiting more frequently.

strategies.title: Interleave Topics, Don't Block
strategies.summary: Kornell and Bjork found mixing topics produces stronger retention than finishing one before moving to the next. Blocked practice feels organised; it produces weaker retention. Discriminating is the mechanism.
strategies.tech: shuffled quiz or random question tool

strategies.title: The Retrieval Schedule
strategies.summary: Dunlosky's review ranked re-reading among the least effective strategies. Teach students the evidence: study, return after two days, then a week, then a month. Many students do the opposite.

strategies.title: Cumulative Review
strategies.summary: Plan retrieval into your medium-term planning, not just lessons. Bring back earlier content in starters and assessments. When it never reappears, students conclude it no longer matters.

strategies.title: Embrace the Struggle
strategies.summary: Bjork coined desirable difficulties for conditions that slow apparent learning but improve long-term retention. Effortful retrieval is the clearest example. Resist the urge to make it easier.

strategies.title: Remove the Scaffolding
strategies.summary: Retrieval with notes open is reading, not retrieval. Fade support gradually: notes first, then headings only, then nothing. The transition to unaided retrieval is where consolidation happens.
strategies.tech: quiz tool; timed or closed-book mode

strategies.title: Vary the Retrieval Context
strategies.summary: Retrieve the same content in different formats and settings, decontextualising knowledge so it is not tied to one context or format. Harder for students; that is precisely the point.

strategies.title: The Generation Effect
strategies.summary: Slamecka and Graf found generating an answer, even a wrong one, before being told it produces stronger retention than passive exposure. The effort of generation drives encoding, not the accuracy.

strategies.title: Forget Before You Retrieve
strategies.summary: Do not retrieve immediately after teaching. Wait a day, then quiz. Wait a week, then quiz again. The gap between learning and retrieval is where consolidation happens.

strategies.title: Retrieval Beyond Facts
strategies.summary: Factual retrieval builds the schema; higher-order retrieval tests whether students can use it. Secure the foundations first, then push beyond them. Retrieval is not a pub quiz.
strategies.tech: quiz tool with varied question types

strategies.title: Concept Mapping from Memory
strategies.summary: Karpicke and Blunt found concept mapping from memory outperformed re-reading for retention. Not just what students know but how ideas connect. Relational knowledge beats isolated facts.

strategies.title: Retrieval Through Teaching
strategies.summary: The learning happens during preparation, not delivery. Preparing to teach demands complete, organised retrieval. Organising knowledge to explain it is where consolidation occurs.

strategies.title: Cued Recall
strategies.summary: Tulving and Thomson showed retrieval depends on available cues. A heading, a keyword, labels removed: each triggers retrieval without doing the work. Builds confidence before unaided retrieval.
strategies.tech: cloze quiz or gapped handout tool

strategies.title: Teach the Illusion of Knowing
strategies.summary: Show students their own illusion of knowing. Ask them to rate confidence before revealing the answer. When they were certain and wrong, that is the precise moment to intervene.

strategies.title: Provide Instant Feedback
strategies.summary: Metcalfe shows instant feedback is essential for confident errors. For general retrieval, allow a processing gap before revealing answers. Speed matters most when confidence is highest.
strategies.tech: quiz tool with instant answer reveal

strategies.title: Confidence Ratings
strategies.summary: Dunlosky and Metcalfe showed students are most confident about things most recently read, not things they actually know. Rate confidence after each attempt, then reveal the answer. That gap is the target.

strategies.title: Retrieval Journals
strategies.summary: Zimmerman showed students who monitor their performance make better revision decisions. Log what came back, what did not, and what needs revisiting. It is a map of what to do next.

strategies.title: Study Strategy Audit
strategies.summary: Dunlosky's review rated ten strategies: re-reading scored low; practice testing scored highest. Ask students how they revise, then show them the data. That conversation is the intervention.

name: Retrieval Practice

title: 24 Ways to Embed Formative Assessment in Your Classroom
subtitle: Evidence informed strategies, with or without technology · Rooted in the work of Black, Wiliam, Butler, Sadler, Berger, Hattie, Bjork, Rosenshine, Angelo & Cross and CAST
scholars: Rooted in the work of Black, Wiliam, Butler, Sadler, Berger, Hattie, Bjork, Rosenshine, Angelo & Cross and CAST
quote: "We should view technology as a tool to amplify good teaching practices, not replace them." — Mark Anderson, RISE Edu Magazine
research: Rooted in the work of Black, Wiliam, Butler, Sadler, Berger, Hattie, Bjork, Rosenshine, Angelo & Cross and CAST

clusters.label: Students as Owners of Their Learning

strategies.title: Separate Intention from Task
strategies.summary: The learning intention is what to learn, not what to do. Finishing the task is not the same as achieving the learning. Keep them distinct in your planning and in what you say to students at every stage of the lesson.

strategies.title: Build Success Criteria Together
strategies.summary: Ask students what excellent looks like before they begin. Their language, not yours, becomes the standard. Criteria they articulate themselves land far more deeply than criteria handed to them.

strategies.title: Exemplars Before Rubrics
strategies.summary: Show work at different standards before students start their own. Students spot quality in someone else's work more readily than in their own. A rubric tells students what quality is; an exemplar shows them.

strategies.title: Withhold the Objective
strategies.summary: Ask students to name what they learned at the end rather than copy an objective at the start. Generating the answer embeds it far more reliably than copying from the board.

strategies.title: Hinge Questions
strategies.summary: A hinge question is a diagnostic question at a lesson turning point. Wrong answers each map to a known misconception. Responses tell you whether to move on or go back. Never improvise it.

strategies.title: Plausible Distractors
strategies.summary: Engineer wrong answers as carefully as the right one. Each distractor should map to a real misconception. Every wrong answer a student gives tells you something precise. Wrong answers are the diagnostic data.

strategies.title: Deliberate Cold Call
strategies.summary: Select who answers deliberately, not at random. Track participation so nobody stays invisible across lessons. Where appropriate, target the students whose thinking you most need to hear.

strategies.title: Mini Whiteboards
strategies.summary: All students write their response and hold it up simultaneously. The teacher reads the room in seconds: full participation, no waiting, no dominant voices. Works across all subjects.

strategies.title: ABCD Response Cards
strategies.summary: Give each student a card: A, B, C and D. Pose a question and all students hold up their answer at once. No hands, no opt-out. The spread of responses shows instantly where misconceptions lie.

strategies.title: Every Voice, Every Time
strategies.summary: Eliciting evidence only works if every student can respond. Offer written, verbal, visual and digital means of expression. The method you choose decides who gets to show what they know.

strategies.title: Think, Pair, Share: Disciplined
strategies.summary: Individual thinking first; paired discussion second; nominated response third. Nomination makes the report-back evidence, not just the most confident voice. Without it, the share is optional.

strategies.title: Comment Only Marking
strategies.summary: Remove grades from work in progress. Research showed comments alone produced the greatest gains. Adding a score to a comment cancels it out: students read the grade and ignore the feedback entirely.

strategies.title: Feedback Must Cause Thinking
strategies.summary: Feedback must be more work for the recipient than the donor. Pose questions rather than writing corrections. If feedback requires no response from the learner, it is not feedback; it is merely information.

strategies.title: Build In Time to Act
strategies.summary: Feedback with no time to act on it has no value. Begin the next lesson with students reading and responding to feedback before anything new. Time to act is where the learning happens.

strategies.title: Whole Class Feedback
strategies.summary: Record class patterns rather than individual comments: common strengths, recurring errors and two or three next steps. Teach to the gap, not to the individual paper. Workload stays manageable.

strategies.title: 3 Questions, Not Corrections
strategies.summary: Return work with three questions rather than corrections. Students must respond before moving on. Cognitive effort belongs with the learner. Feedback that corrects for them removes the struggle.

strategies.title: Guided Practice Together
strategies.summary: Independence is the destination, not the starting point. Before students work alone, have them practise with peers in structured steps, checking each other's responses at every stage before moving forward.

strategies.title: Student Generated Questions
strategies.summary: Ask students to write questions that could appear in an assessment on this topic. Collate the best and use them for review. Generating questions demands higher order thinking than simply answering them.
strategies.tech: shared doc or quiz builder tool

strategies.title: Structured Peer Assessment
strategies.summary: Peer feedback only works when students understand quality. Use exemplars first so students assess against shared criteria. Without shared criteria, peer feedback is opinion, not evidence.

strategies.title: Spaced Retrieval Practice
strategies.summary: Low stakes quizzing on prior content, not today's lesson. Returning to older material at increasing intervals is one of the most robust findings in memory research. Re-reading notes is not the same as retrieving.

strategies.title: Test Before You Teach
strategies.summary: Quiz students on material before you teach it. Triggering the feeling of not knowing primes attention and improves retention. Students who struggle before instruction remember the answer better.

strategies.title: The Muddiest Point
strategies.summary: At lesson close, each student anonymously writes the one thing they are least clear about. The teacher addresses the most common muddy points publicly at the start of the next lesson. Two minutes; high value.

strategies.title: Review Little and Often
strategies.summary: Begin every lesson with a brief review of prior content: yesterday's, last week's, last month's. The most effective teachers check understanding constantly. If most students cannot answer, adjust the pace of teaching.

strategies.title: Spaced Self Quizzing
strategies.summary: Teach students to quiz themselves rather than re-read notes. Re-reading feels productive but produces weak retention. Self quizzing feels harder but works. Retrieval effort drives long term memory.

name: Formative Assessment

title: 24 Ways to Embed Effective Feedback in Your Classroom
subtitle: Evidence-informed strategies, with or without technology
scholars: Rooted in the work of Hattie & Timperley, Sadler, Butler, Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, Wiliam, Kluger & DeNisi, Shute, Topping, Andrade, Carless and Boud
quote: "Feedback is one of the most powerful influences on learning and achievement, but this impact can be either positive or negative." — Hattie & Timperley, 2007
research: Rooted in the work of Hattie & Timperley, Sadler, Butler, Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, Wiliam, Kluger & DeNisi, Shute, Topping, Andrade, Carless and Boud

strategies.title: Feedback Is Not Marking
strategies.summary: If a student never reads or acts on your comments, you have marked but not given feedback. Before returning work, plan how students will engage with it. No engagement, no feedback.
strategies.tech: audio or digital ink feedback tool

strategies.title: Feed Up, Feed Back, Feed Forward
strategies.summary: Every comment should answer three questions: where am I going, how am I doing, what next? Most feedback answers only the second. Check yours covers all three before you hand it back.

strategies.title: Four Levels of Feedback
strategies.summary: Before writing a comment, ask: am I addressing the task, the process or the person? Task and process feedback improve learning. Self-level praise undermines it. Name your target.

strategies.title: One Third Makes It Worse
strategies.summary: Over a third of feedback interventions decrease performance. Before giving feedback, check: does this comment address the work or the student? If it is about the student, rewrite it.

strategies.title: Sadler's Three Conditions
strategies.summary: Share the criteria before students begin. Show them how to compare their work against it. Give them time to act on what they find. Without all three steps, feedback cannot function.

strategies.title: Immediate for Simple Tasks
strategies.summary: For simple or procedural tasks, correct errors immediately. Shute found quick feedback prevents mistakes from embedding. Do not wait until next lesson to fix what can be fixed now.

strategies.title: Delayed for Complex Tasks
strategies.summary: For complex work, a short delay before feedback lets the learner process first. Immediate correction on difficult tasks can short-circuit thinking. Let the struggle do its work.

strategies.title: During, Not Just After
strategies.summary: Feedback given while students are still working is formative. Feedback returned weeks later is a post-mortem. Move around the room, intervene in the moment. Proximity is strategy.

strategies.title: Comment Only, No Grades
strategies.summary: Butler found comments alone produced the greatest gains. A grade cancels the comment: students see the score and skip the words. If grades are mandated, delay until feedback is used.

strategies.title: Reduce Volume, Raise Focus
strategies.summary: A page of comments overwhelms. One or two precise targets land. Identify the one thing that would make the biggest difference right now and focus entirely on that.

strategies.title: Peer Feedback with Structure
strategies.summary: Give students criteria and a protocol before they assess each other's work. Topping showed peer feedback improves learning for both, but without scaffolding it becomes empty praise.
strategies.tech: peer review tool with criteria prompts

strategies.title: Self-Assessment as Process
strategies.summary: Ask students to assess their work against criteria before you mark it. Andrade found the act of comparing, not the accuracy of the judgment, improves performance. Process is the point.

strategies.title: Dialogic Feedback
strategies.summary: Build reply loops into feedback. Let students question and clarify comments over time rather than receive a final judgment. Carless showed uptake rises when feedback is a conversation.

strategies.title: Technology as Feedback Source
strategies.summary: Use automated tools for factual accuracy and procedural correctness; reserve your time for voice, argument and creativity. Match the feedback source to what is being assessed.

strategies.title: Whole Class Feedback
strategies.summary: Read the set and identify patterns: common strengths, recurring errors, one priority next step. Teach to the gap, not to each paper. Sustainable for teachers; precise for students.

strategies.title: Task, Not Person
strategies.summary: Feedback that threatens self-concept decreases performance. "This paragraph needs restructuring" works. "You need to try harder" does not. Direct feedback at the work, not the person.

strategies.title: Feedback Must Cause Thinking
strategies.summary: Write "why might this be stronger with evidence?" not insert the evidence yourself. If feedback needs no effort from the learner, it is information, not feedback. Thinking is the point.

strategies.title: Praise the Strategy, Not the Trait
strategies.summary: Butler found task-involving feedback improves performance. Ego-involving feedback shifts attention from learning to self-image. Praise what the student did, not who the student is.

strategies.title: Build Feedback Literacy
strategies.summary: Teach students how to read and act on feedback before you give it. Model with an exemplar: here is the comment, what it means, what to do next. Feedback literacy is taught, not assumed.

strategies.title: Seven Principles of Good Practice
strategies.summary: Audit your practice against Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's seven principles. Do you clarify criteria? Enable self-assessment? Encourage dialogue? Close the gap? Redesign where you do not.

strategies.title: Build In Time to Act
strategies.summary: Feedback with no time to act on it is wasted. Begin the next lesson with students reading and responding to comments before anything new. The response is the learning event.

strategies.title: Questions, Not Corrections
strategies.summary: Return work with questions, not corrections. "What evidence supports this claim?" demands more thinking than rewriting it for them. The cognitive work belongs with the learner.

strategies.title: Sustainable Feedback
strategies.summary: Boud argues feedback should build the learner's capacity to judge quality. If students always need you to tell them how they did, the system has failed. Design for independence.

strategies.title: Feedback as Design, Not Event
strategies.summary: Plan feedback into your scheme of work: who gives it, when, in what form, and when students act on it. Feedback designed into learning from the start works. Left to chance, it does not.

name: Feedback

title: 24 Ways to Embed Effective Questioning & Discussion in Your Classroom
subtitle: Evidence-informed strategies, with or without technology · Rooted in cognitive and educational research
scholars: Rooted in the work of Anderson & Krathwohl, Dillon, Hattie & Zierer, Rowe, Tobin, Lyman, Wiliam, Good & Brophy, Alexander, Mercer, Michaels, O’Connor & Resnick, and King
quote: “Classroom talk is the most pervasive but arguably the least examined tool in any teacher’s repertoire.” — Robin Alexander
research: Rooted in the work of Anderson & Krathwohl, Dillon, Hattie & Zierer, Rowe, Tobin, Lyman, Wiliam, Good & Brophy, Alexander, Mercer, Michaels, O’Connor & Resnick, and King

strategies.title: Questions That Make Thinking Visible
strategies.summary: Anderson and Krathwohl map six levels: remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, evaluating, creating. These are not a hierarchy of worth. Recall is foundational, not inferior.
strategies.tech: question bank or lesson planning tool

strategies.title: Surface, Deep and Transfer
strategies.summary: Hattie and Zierer distinguish surface (what), deep (why) and transfer questions. Each serves a different stage. Reaching transfer before surface is secure sets students up to fail.
strategies.tech: discussion prompt or slide display tool

strategies.title: Open Questions Demand More
strategies.summary: Dillon found genuine open questions, where the teacher does not know the answer, produce the most extended student reasoning. Not every question needs a predetermined destination.

strategies.title: Plan Questions Before the Lesson
strategies.summary: Improvised questions default to recall, not because recall is wrong but because planning stops there. Anderson and Krathwohl works as a planning tool: write questions at every level.
strategies.tech: lesson planning or slide preparation tool

strategies.title: Alternatives to Questions
strategies.summary: Dillon found statements and silence elicit richer responses than questions. Try: Tell me more. I had not considered that. Not every probe needs to end with a question mark.

strategies.title: Wait Time 1: After You Ask
strategies.summary: Rowe found most teachers wait under one second before speaking. Extending to three seconds increases the length and complexity of responses. Silence is thinking, not a gap to fill.

strategies.title: Wait Time 2: After a Student Speaks
strategies.summary: Rowe identified a second wait time: the pause after a student responds. Three seconds prompts elaboration and self-correction. Silence after an answer signals that more is expected.
strategies.tech: live polling or response capture tool

strategies.title: Write Before You Speak
strategies.summary: Ask students to write before any verbal response is taken. Writing prevents the quickest from foreclosing others’ thinking. The pen democratises the room before the voice takes over.
strategies.tech: shared doc, whiteboard or response tool

strategies.title: Think-Pair-Share
strategies.summary: Lyman’s think-pair-share gives every student thinking time before public exposure. Pairs test ideas with a peer first. The result is more considered and more substantive discussion.
strategies.tech: partner chat tool or response system

strategies.title: Hands Down
strategies.summary: Wiliam shows hand-raising distorts who answers. A small group volunteers repeatedly; the rest disengage. Remove hands and direct to named students. Every student should be asked.
strategies.tech: random name picker or class list tool

strategies.title: Cold Call Without Threat
strategies.summary: Good and Brophy showed differential questioning reinforces attainment gaps. Direct questions are equitable only when the climate supports it. Norms: no wrong attempts, only thinking.
strategies.tech: random selector or seating plan tool

strategies.title: Track Who You Ask
strategies.summary: Good and Brophy found teachers direct harder questions to higher-attaining students. Track participation across lessons. Patterns invisible in the moment become visible on paper.

strategies.title: Pose, Pause, Pounce, Bounce
strategies.summary: Wiliam’s PPPB: pose the question, pause, direct to one student, then bounce the answer to another. The bounce keeps all students alert and spreads thinking across the whole room.

strategies.title: Five Principles of Dialogic Talk
strategies.summary: Alexander identifies five qualities of dialogic talk: collective, reciprocal, supportive, cumulative and purposeful. Most talk meets two or three of these. Audit and start with the gaps.

strategies.title: Break the IRE Pattern
strategies.summary: IRE (Initiation, Response, Evaluation): ask, answer, judge. Alexander shows this pattern limits thinking. Replace evaluation with a follow-up question. What makes you say that?
strategies.tech: video reflection or lesson capture tool

strategies.title: Exploratory Talk
strategies.summary: Mercer distinguishes disputational, cumulative and exploratory talk. Only exploratory talk, where students challenge ideas with evidence and build on each thinking, improves outcomes.

strategies.title: Ground Rules for Talk
strategies.summary: Mercer found teaching norms of exploratory talk transforms discussion. Norms co-constructed with the class outperform those displayed or modelled. Make the ground rules together.

strategies.title: Accountable Talk
strategies.summary: Michaels, O’Connor and Resnick hold students to accurate knowledge and rigorous reasoning. Teach moves: I agree because..., The evidence is..., Say more.... Language shapes thinking.

strategies.title: Build on Student Responses
strategies.summary: Alexander’s EEF programme showed gains when teachers extended rather than evaluated. Return an answer: Aisha says X. Does anyone want to add or challenge? Conductor, not judge.
strategies.tech: live display or response capture tool

strategies.title: Teach Question Stems
strategies.summary: King found students trained to generate questions using stems produce richer discussion than those answering only teacher questions. Generating questions demands deeper processing.
strategies.tech: question stem cards or display tool

strategies.title: Reciprocal Peer Questioning
strategies.summary: King’s reciprocal questioning has students generate and pose questions to each other, with neither knowing the answer. This produces genuine enquiry rather than rehearsal. Aim to think.

strategies.title: Questions as Evidence of Understanding
strategies.summary: A student’s question reveals the depth of their understanding. Ask for one written question before leaving. Why does X cause Y? shows far more than What is X?. Questions are windows.

strategies.title: Interthinking Through Questions
strategies.summary: Mercer’s interthinking describes shared cognition built through language. Student questions sustain joint enquiry. The goal is thinking in common, not performance for the teacher.

strategies.title: Questions That Drive Enquiry
strategies.summary: King found connecting questions to prior knowledge produces the most powerful learning. Ask students to write what they know and want to know. Their questions become the entry point.
strategies.tech: shared doc, padlet or survey tool

name: Questioning & Discussion

title: 24 Ways to Embed Effective Explanations & Modelling in Your Classroom
subtitle: Evidence-informed strategies, with or without technology · Rooted in cognitive and educational research
scholars: Rooted in the work of Rosenshine, Sweller, Mayer, Paivio, Willingham, Atkinson, and the EEF Digital Technology Guidance (2019)
quote: “To improve learning, technology must be used in a way that is informed by effective pedagogy.” — EEF, 2019
research: Rooted in the work of Rosenshine, Sweller, Mayer, Paivio, Willingham, Atkinson, and the EEF Digital Technology Guidance (2019)

strategies.title: Small Steps, Always
strategies.summary: Rosenshine: present new material in small steps with practice after each. Use animations to chunk information and reveal content gradually. Let students process before continuing.

strategies.title: Concrete Before Abstract
strategies.summary: Willingham: anchor new ideas to concrete examples first. Use images, video or objects to make the abstract visible before naming it. Move to the abstract once the concrete is secure.

strategies.title: Connect to Prior Knowledge
strategies.summary: Rosenshine: connect to prior knowledge before introducing anything new. Use a retrieval starter or concept map on screen to activate what students know. Link before you launch.

strategies.title: Clarity Over Novelty
strategies.summary: The EEF found clarity matters more than delivery method. A diagram under a visualiser can outperform a polished video. Choose the tool that makes the idea clearest, not the newest.
strategies.tech: any display tool used with purpose

strategies.title: Check, Don’t Assume
strategies.summary: Listening is not learning. Use live polls or mini whiteboards to check understanding at every step. Rosenshine: reteach before moving on. The explanation is the start, not the finish.
strategies.tech: live polling or mini whiteboard tool

strategies.title: Supplement, Never Substitute
strategies.summary: The EEF: technology works best when it supplements teaching, not replaces it. A screencast works alongside classroom explanation, not instead of it. Supplement, never substitute.

strategies.title: Four Slots, No More
strategies.summary: Sweller: working memory holds about four items. Every screen element competes for those slots. Strip slides to essentials. Press B to blank the screen when you want attention on you.

strategies.title: Avoid Split Attention
strategies.summary: Sweller’s split attention: separate text and diagrams force learners to search between them. Integrate labels directly into the image. Use annotation tools to build the diagram live.

strategies.title: Say It or Show It, Not Both
strategies.summary: Sweller’s redundancy effect: narrating text on screen forces double processing. Say it or show it, not both. Use the B or W key to blank the slide while you talk through the idea.
strategies.tech: B/W key in PowerPoint or Keynote

strategies.title: Remove the Clutter
strategies.summary: Mayer’s coherence: remove every word, image and sound that does not support learning. Strip clip art from slides. Cut background music. Every element on screen must earn its place.

strategies.title: Signal What Matters
strategies.summary: Mayer’s signalling: bold, arrows and highlights direct attention to what matters. Use annotation tools to signal live during the explanation. Without it, learners search alone.

strategies.title: Chunk and Reveal
strategies.summary: Mayer’s segmenting: break content into chunks. Use slide animations to reveal one idea per click, not auto-play. Let working memory process before the next chunk arrives.

strategies.title: Words and Images Together
strategies.summary: Paivio’s dual coding: the brain processes words and images through separate channels. Design every slide with both: a key visual paired with minimal text. Two routes to the same idea.

strategies.title: Narrate, Don’t Label
strategies.summary: Mayer’s modality: people learn better from images with narration than images with text. Record a narrated screencast over a diagram. Let the voice do what text would overload.

strategies.title: Keep Words Near Images
strategies.summary: Mayer’s spatial contiguity: place words near the images they describe. Labels sit beside the diagram, not in a separate list. Use slide design to keep related information together.

strategies.title: Progressive Reveal
strategies.summary: Use animations to reveal content one step at a time. One idea per click, building the full picture gradually. Progressive reveal aligns the display to the pace of your explanation.

strategies.title: Short Screencasts
strategies.summary: Record short screencasts with narration over visuals. Mayer: images plus voice outperforms text-heavy slides. Keep each video to one idea. Brevity beats completeness every time.
strategies.tech: screen recording tool; Loom or similar

strategies.title: Pre-Train the Vocabulary
strategies.summary: Mayer’s pre-training: teach key terms before the main explanation. A vocabulary slide or pre-lesson video builds familiarity first. Learners who know the words can focus on the ideas.

strategies.title: Think Aloud
strategies.summary: Rosenshine: model the process, not the product. Use a visualiser or screen share to think aloud live. Narrate your decisions as you work. Make invisible expertise visible to all.

strategies.title: The Visualiser as Stage
strategies.summary: A visualiser turns any desk into a modelling stage. Show handwriting, annotate text, build diagrams under the camera. The EEF found this among the most promising classroom technology.

strategies.title: Worked Examples on Replay
strategies.summary: Sweller and Cooper: students learn more from worked examples than equivalent problems. Record a screencast of the example so students can pause and study the method at their pace.

strategies.title: Alternate Examples and Practice
strategies.summary: Atkinson: alternate worked examples with practice. Display an example on screen, then set a parallel task. Example, try. Example, try. Interleaving builds understanding faster.
strategies.tech: display and task alternating on screen

strategies.title: Fade the Scaffolds
strategies.summary: Rosenshine: begin with full support, then fade. Show a complete example, then a partial one with gaps, then independent practice. Use fillable templates to structure the fading.

strategies.title: Simulations Beyond Physical Limits
strategies.summary: The EEF found simulations let students manipulate variables and see consequences beyond physical limits. Use to extend your explanation, not replace it. Technology serves pedagogy.

name: Explanations & Modelling

title: 24 Ways to Embed Metacognition & Self-Regulation in Your Classroom
subtitle: Evidence-informed strategies, with or without technology · Rooted in cognitive and educational research
scholars: Rooted in the work of Zimmerman, Flavell, Winne, Butler, and Willingham
quote: “As children should learn about metacognition and how best to learn, they should also be taught how to use technology to support their learning.” — Anderson & Lewis, The EdTech Playbook, 2025
research: Rooted in the work of Zimmerman, Flavell, Winne, Butler, and Willingham

strategies.title: Set the Goal First
strategies.summary: Zimmerman: planning begins with a specific, proximal goal, not a vague aim. Have students state what a good answer to this question looks like before they start writing it.

strategies.title: Knowledge Comes First
strategies.summary: Willingham: you cannot plan or monitor a task you know nothing about. Teach the content first; metacognition works on knowledge, never instead of it. Build the base, then regulate.
strategies.tech: retrieval starter to check the base

strategies.title: Analyse the Task First
strategies.summary: Zimmerman: strong learners break a task into its demands before starting. Ask students what this question is really asking and which prior topics it draws on before they answer.
strategies.tech: annotate the question on a board

strategies.title: Pick a Strategy on Purpose
strategies.summary: Flavell: planning means selecting an approach, not defaulting to one. Have students name which method they will use for this problem and why, before the first line goes down.
strategies.tech: strategy menu in a shared doc

strategies.title: Build Realistic Confidence
strategies.summary: Zimmerman: self-efficacy drives effort, but it must be earned by past success, not pep talks. Point students to a recent task they mastered to set a credible expectation for this one.
strategies.tech: portfolio of prior work to revisit

strategies.title: Check, Don't Just Feel
strategies.summary: Winne: a novice's sense of understanding is unreliable. Pair every self-check with an external test, a quiz or worked answer, so monitoring rests on evidence rather than confidence.

strategies.title: Scaffold Focus, Then Fade
strategies.summary: Zimmerman: monitoring needs a low-distraction environment first. Use classroom.cloud to scaffold focus while students are learning, then withdraw it as they manage attention themselves.

strategies.title: Build in Stop Points
strategies.summary: Winne: monitoring fades without prompts. Insert planned pauses where students ask whether the approach is still working, before sunk effort makes a wrong method hard to abandon.

strategies.title: Ask Yourself As You Go
strategies.summary: Flavell: monitoring means questioning your understanding mid-task. Teach students to pause and ask “do I actually understand this?”, so gaps surface in time to fix them.

strategies.title: Make Thinking Visible
strategies.summary: Flavell: regulation you cannot see, you cannot coach. Have students leave a brief trace of their reasoning as they work, so you and they can inspect the process, not just the product.
strategies.tech: shared doc showing working e.g. OneNote

strategies.title: Judge Against a Standard
strategies.summary: Zimmerman: self-judgement needs a reference, not a hunch. Give students the mark scheme or an exemplar to compare their work against, so evaluation is anchored to a real standard.

strategies.title: Credit the Method, Not the Gift
strategies.summary: Zimmerman: how students explain a result shapes the next attempt. Steer attribution toward the method used, which they can change, rather than fixed ability, which they cannot.

strategies.title: Turn Reflection Into a Plan
strategies.summary: Butler: feedback only regulates learning if it changes the next action. Have students convert each reflection into one concrete adjustment they will make on the very next task.

strategies.title: Compare Predicted to Actual
strategies.summary: Winne: calibration improves when students see the gap between expected and real scores. Have them predict a mark, then compare, so monitoring is corrected by evidence over time.

strategies.title: Reflection Feeds Teaching
strategies.summary: Butler: self-regulation and instruction are a loop. Use what students notice about their own errors to decide what you reteach, so their reflection shapes the next lesson.

strategies.title: Know the Strategy Itself
strategies.summary: Flavell: students cannot deploy a strategy they have never been taught. Teach retrieval, spacing or self-explanation explicitly as named methods before expecting independent use.

strategies.title: Know When to Use Each
strategies.summary: Winne: conditional knowledge, knowing which strategy suits which task, is what separates skilled learners. Teach not just the method but the cues that signal when it is the right one.

strategies.title: Fade the Scaffold
strategies.summary: Zimmerman: support must be withdrawn for self-regulation to develop. Move from modelled to guided to independent use, removing prompts as students show they no longer need them.

strategies.title: Keep What Works, Drop the Rest
strategies.summary: Winne: learners refine an approach by checking whether it worked. Have students trial a study method, judge it against results, and keep only what the evidence supports.

strategies.title: Tie Strategies to Content
strategies.summary: Willingham: strategies do not float free of subjects. Teach each one inside the content it serves, so students learn to self-regulate this topic, not metacognition in the abstract.

strategies.title: Schedule Your Own Spacing
strategies.summary: Regulating when you study is a planning act. Teach students to set their own calendar reminders to revisit topics over time, owning the spacing rather than waiting to be told.

strategies.title: Make Your Own Questions
strategies.summary: Writing a good question forces you to judge what matters. Have students build low-stakes quizzes and flashcards from their own notes, so the tool supports retrieval they have authored.

strategies.title: Regulate the Device Too
strategies.summary: Self-regulation now includes the screen. Teach students to use focus modes and silence alerts as a deliberate choice, regulating the tool so it serves attention instead of stealing it.

strategies.title: Partner, Not Substitute
strategies.summary: Willingham: memory is the residue of thought. Offload the thinking to AI and nothing is learned. Have students use it to check and challenge their reasoning, not to do it for them.
strategies.tech: AI as a critic of own work
